## TL;DR

Photosynthesis is two reactions in series, not one. The light reactions split water and turn sunlight into ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle spends that energy fixing $\text{CO}_2$ into sugar, using an enzyme, RuBisCO, that also reacts with oxygen and wastes a fifth of what it fixes. Every carbon a blueberry bush ever turns into fruit passed through this leaf first.
:::

## The light reactions: splitting water for electrons

In the thylakoid membrane, a photon strikes photosystem II and knocks an electron loose. The gap left behind is filled by ripping a water molecule apart:

$$2\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4e^-$$

The oxygen you breathe is a waste product of this step. The freed electrons run downhill through an electron transport chain to photosystem I, get re-energised by a second photon, and end up reducing $\text{NADP}^+$ to $\text{NADPH}$. The proton gradient built up along the way drives ATP synthase, the same rotary mechanism that runs mitochondrial respiration in reverse. Two products leave the thylakoid membrane: $\text{ATP}$ and $\text{NADPH}$, both spent in the next step, neither storable for later.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    L["Sunlight"] --> PSII["Photosystem II<br/>splits H₂O → O₂"]
    PSII --> ETC["Electron transport chain<br/>builds H⁺ gradient"]
    ETC --> PSI["Photosystem I<br/>re-energises electron"]
    PSI --> Products["ATP + NADPH"]
    Products --> Calvin["Calvin cycle<br/>fixes CO₂ into sugar"]
    Calvin -->|"RuBP regenerated"| Calvin

    class L ochre
    class PSII indigo
    class ETC plum
    class PSI indigo
    class Products olive
    class Calvin sage
```

## The Calvin cycle: an enzyme that fixes carbon, and sometimes doesn't

In the stroma, the enzyme RuBisCO attaches a $\text{CO}_2$ molecule to a five-carbon sugar, RuBP, producing two molecules of a three-carbon compound. Spending the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions turns those into G3P, the sugar the plant actually uses; most of the G3P cycles back to regenerate RuBP, and one in six leaves the cycle to become glucose, starch or sucrose.

$$6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{light reactions}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2$$

RuBisCO is the least selective enzyme a plant depends on. It cannot fully distinguish $\text{CO}_2$ from $\text{O}_2$, and on a hot, dry day, when stomata close to save water and $\text{CO}_2$ inside the leaf runs low relative to oxygen, RuBisCO increasingly grabs $\text{O}_2$ instead. That side reaction, photorespiration, consumes energy and releases $\text{CO}_2$ the plant just fixed, with no sugar to show for it. Blueberries, like most temperate crops, run this pathway unmodified, called $\text{C}_3$ photosynthesis for the three-carbon compound RuBisCO produces. Under typical conditions photorespiration burns off somewhere around a fifth of what the Calvin cycle fixes. It is not a defect to be designed around later in this series; it is the tax every $\text{C}_3$ leaf already pays, and it is why closing stomata under heat or drought costs more than just lost $\text{CO}_2$.

## Key takeaways

- The light reactions split water, releasing oxygen as a byproduct, and convert light energy into ATP and NADPH.
- The Calvin cycle spends that ATP and NADPH to fix $\text{CO}_2$ into sugar, using the enzyme RuBisCO.
- RuBisCO also reacts with oxygen instead of $\text{CO}_2$, a wasteful side reaction called photorespiration that intensifies when stomata close under heat or drought.
- Every gram of fruit a bush grows is downstream of this leaf-level chemistry; the next module turns it into a whole-plant carbon budget.
